keyVerseText: Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.
rootMeaning: γεύομαι (geúomai) is a primary Greek verb fundamentally meaning 'to taste' or 'to eat.' Its root sense involves the physical act of tasting, which naturally extends to eating, but it also carries a figurative dimension of experiencing something firsthand, whether good or ill. This literal sensory action enriches the English gloss by emphasizing direct, personal encounter rather than mere intellectual acknowledgment.
usageInScripture: The word appears fifteen times in the New Testament, consistently conveying both literal and metaphorical senses of tasting or experiencing. Top translations include 'shall,' 'have tasted,' and 'shall taste,' indicating a nuanced use often involving future or completed actions. This range shows the word's flexibility in expressing not only physical eating but also the experiential knowledge of spiritual realities or trials.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding γεύομαι as both tasting and experiencing deepens our grasp of biblical teaching about faith and spiritual life. It conveys that believers are called not just to know about God abstractly but to 'taste' or personally experience His presence, grace, and power. This verb underscores the reality that faith involves intimate, tangible encounters with God’s kingdom, suffering, and salvation. It reminds Christians that their spiritual journey includes real participation and experiential knowledge, not mere doctrine.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 16:28, Jesus says some standing there 'shall not taste of death till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.' The use of γεύομαι here highlights the experiential nature of death—not just its occurrence but the personal 'tasting' or undergoing of it. Jesus promises that certain disciples will not personally experience death before witnessing His kingdom, emphasizing the immediacy and reality of that coming event. This enriches the verse by portraying death as something to be personally encountered, which some will be spared temporarily.
